                                       I.     BACKGROUND
                                   1
                                              A.      Factual Background
                                   2
                                              The Court has described the factual background of this case in prior orders (see, e.g., ECF
                                   3
                                       No. 57) but finds it appropriate to briefly touch upon some points relevant to the analysis of the
                                   4
                                       instant motion. This case involves Eric and Sandra Olson’s (the “Olsons”) departure from their
                                   5
                                       former employer, WFG, and creation of their new competing company, GFI. WFG requires its
                                   6
                                       agents to sign an agreement (the “Agent Agreement”) that contains provisions that the Olsons
                                   7
                                       contend are unlawfully restrictive (the so-called “Restrictive Covenants”). In addition to the
                                   8
                                       Agent Agreement, WFG required the Olsons—and presumably all WFG agents—to sign
                                   9
                                       agreements to arbitrate claims between them. See Arbitration Agreement, ECF No. 192-5.
                                  10
                                       Specifically, agents agreed “to use binding arbitration as the means to resolve all disputes that may
                                  11
                                       arise out of or relate to [their] relationship with WFG.” Id. at 1.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                              B.      Procedural Background
                                  13
                                              This case began on January 25, 2024, when WFG filed a complaint against the Olsons in
                                  14
                                       Santa Clara County Superior Court. Mrs. Olson and GFI filed suit against WFG in this Court the
                                  15
                                       same day (Sandra Olson, et al., v. World Fin. Grp. Ins. Agency, LLC, Case No. 5:24-cv-00477
                                  16
                                       (N.D. Cal.)). The following day, Mr. Olson filed another lawsuit against WFG (Eric Olson v.
                                  17
                                       World Fin. Grp. Ins. Agency, LLC, et al., Case No. 5:24-cv-00481 (N.D. Cal.)) and removed
                                  18
                                       WFG’s complaint to this Court (World Fin. Grp. Ins. Agency, LLC v. Olson, et al., Case No. 5:24-
                                  19
                                       cv-00480 (N.D. Cal), ECF No. 1). The Court later consolidated the three cases and designated the
                                  20
                                       above-captioned action as the lead case. ECF No. 58. As all of this was happening, WFG filed
                                  21
                                       another complaint against GFI in the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming. World Fin.
                                  22
                                       Grp. Ins. Agency, LLC v. Global Fin. Impact, LLC, Case No. 1:24-cv-00019 (D. Wyo.). WFG
                                  23
                                       later dismissed those claims voluntarily.
                                  24
                                              On July 19, 2024, the Court granted WFG’s motion to compel the claims between it and
                                  25
                                       the Olsons to arbitration, except for both parties’ claims for injunctive relief—relief squarely
                                  26
                                       exempted from their Arbitration Agreement. Case No. 24-cv-00481, ECF No. 67; Case No. 24-
                                  27

                                   1   cv-00477, ECF No. 56. The claims GFI brought against WFG in its third amended complaint

                                   2   were also not compelled to arbitration at that time, because GFI was not a party to any arbitration

                                   3   agreement with WFG. See Third Am. Compl., ECF No. 179. On December 19, 2024, the Olsons

                                   4   served WFG with an arbitration demand asserting breach of the Agent Agreement, violation of

                                   5   Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600, unfair competition, tortious interference, conversion, and other

                                   6   claims. ECF No. 191-4. WFG then served its own arbitration demand asserting claims for breach

                                   7   of the Agent Agreement, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and

                                   8   tortious interference with contract. ECF No. 198-4.

                                   9          WFG filed counterclaims against GFI on January 17, 2025 (ECF No. 182), and a notice of

                                  10   errata revising those counterclaims a few weeks later (ECF No. 189). On February 7, 2025, the

                                  11   day after WFG filed its notice of errata, GFI filed the instant motion. WFG filed amended

                                  12   counterclaims against GFI two weeks later. First Am. Countercls. (“FACC”), ECF No. 195.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   II.    LEGAL STANDARD
                                  14          The FAA governs the enforceability of contractual arbitration agreements, like the one

                                  15   here. Kramer v. Toyota Motor Corp., 705 F.3d 1122, 1126 (9th Cir. 2013) (citing 9 U.S.C. § 1 et

                                  16   seq.). The FAA reflects both a “liberal federal policy favoring arbitration,” and the “fundamental

                                  17   principle that arbitration is a matter of contract.” AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion, 563 U.S.

                                  18   333, 339 (2011). Pursuant to the latter principle, the contractual right to compel arbitration

                                  19   generally “may not be invoked by one who is not a party to the agreement and does not otherwise

                                  20   possess the right to compel arbitration.” Kramer, 705 F.3d at 1126 (citation omitted). Likewise,

                                  21   “[t]he strong public policy in favor of arbitration does not extend to those who are not parties to an

                                  22   arbitration agreement.” Comedy Club, Inc. v. Improv W. Assocs., 553 F.3d 1277, 1287 (9th Cir.

                                  23   2009) (citation omitted).

                                  24          There is an exception, however. Under the doctrine of equitable estoppel, “a litigant who

                                  25   is not a party to an arbitration agreement may invoke arbitration under the FAA if the relevant

                                  26   state contract law allows the litigant to enforce the agreement.” Kramer, 705 F.3d at 1128 (citing

                                  27   Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle, 556 U.S. 624, 632 (2009)). California law—which neither party

                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION
                                                                                         3
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 247         Filed 09/09/25    Page 4 of 9




                                   1   disputes applies to this action—permits a nonsignatory to enforce an arbitration clause in two

                                   2   circumstances:

                                   3                    (1) when a signatory must rely on the terms of the written agreement
                                                        in asserting its claims against the nonsignatory or the claims
                                   4                    are “intimately founded in and intertwined with” the underlying
                                                        contract, and (2) when the signatory alleges substantially
                                   5                    interdependent and concerted misconduct by the nonsignatory and
                                                        another signatory and “the allegations of interdependent misconduct
                                   6                    [are] founded in or intimately connected with the obligations of the
                                                        underlying agreement.”
                                   7   Id. at 1128–29 (quoting Goldman v. KPMG LLP, 173 Cal. App. 4th 209, 221 (2009)). This rule is
                                   8   grounded in fairness and prevents signatories from seeking to hold nonsignatories liable pursuant
                                   9   to a contract while avoiding an arbitration provision in the same agreement. Pac. Fertility Cases,
                                  10   85 Cal. App. 5th 887, 893 (2022) (citation omitted).
                                  11
                                       III.   DISCUSSION
                                  12          GFI contends that the first prong of the Goldman test applies to WFG’s counterclaims.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   That is, GFI, a nonsignatory to the Agent Agreement and Arbitration Agreement, argues that it
                                  14   may nonetheless invoke the latter because (1) WFG must rely on the terms of the Agent
                                  15   Agreement to assert its counterclaims, and (2) the counterclaims are founded in and intertwined
                                  16   with the obligations imposed by the Agent Agreement. Mot. at 20–23. The Court analyzes
                                  17   whether WFG is equitably estopped from avoiding arbitration under this framework but begins by
                                  18   addressing a threshold procedural issue concerning WFG’s counterclaims.
                                  19
                                              A.        Amendment of Counterclaims
                                  20          In its motion, GFI characterizes WFG’s counterclaims against GFI (ECF No. 182) as the
                                  21   “Fourth Amended Counterclaims,” or “4ACC.” See Mot. at 12. GFI argues that WFG filed this
                                  22   amendment without leave of the Court or GFI as required by the Federal Rules. WFG denies that
                                  23   its counterclaims are an amendment to any pre-existing claims in this action and contends that it
                                  24   was not required to seek leave because its counterclaims are permissive rather than compulsory.
                                  25   Opp. at 10–13.
                                  26          Subject to few exceptions, a party must state as a compulsory counterclaim any claim that
                                  27   it has against the opposing party that arises out of the same transaction or occurrence and does not
                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD          Document 247          Filed 09/09/25   Page 5 of 9




                                   1   require adding another party over whom the Court does not have jurisdiction. Fed. R. Civ. P.

                                   2   13(a). Compulsory counterclaims are forfeited if not raised in an answer. All other counterclaims

                                   3   are permissive and may be filed later. Fed. R. Civ. P. 13(b). Once the period to amend as a matter

                                   4   of course has passed, a party may amend its pleading only with the opposing party’s written

                                   5   consent or leave of court. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2).

                                   6          GFI does not dispute WFG’s assertion that WFG’s counterclaims are permissive. See

                                   7   Reply. Instead, it argues that WFG’s claims against the Olsons constitute earlier-filed

                                   8   counterclaims against GFI. Mot. at 16 (citing Case No. 5:24-cv-00480, ECF Nos. 1, 72). But GFI

                                   9   provides no authority to support that reasoning. WFG’s counterclaims are different from claims it

                                  10   has previously asserted and are directed against GFI as opposed to the Olsons, so the

                                  11   counterclaims do not appear to be an improper attempt to amend any of WFG’s existing claims.

                                  12   The Court will therefore not construe WFG’s initial filing of counterclaims (ECF No. 182) as an
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   amendment. Nor does the Court construe WFG’s notice of errata (ECF No. 189) as an

                                  14   amendment subject to Rule 15’s requirements. By that logic, Mr. Olson’s own notice of errata for

                                  15   his first amended complaint against WFG would have been an improper second amendment to the

                                  16   complaint. See Case No. 5:24-cv-00481, ECF No. 27. And even if WFG’s errata were considered

                                  17   an amendment, it was timely filed within the deadline to amend as a matter of course. See Fed. R.

                                  18   Civ. P. 15(a)(1).

                                  19          On February 20, 2025, during the pendency of the instant motion seeking to dismiss

                                  20   WFG’s initial counterclaims, WFG filed its “First Amended Counterclaims.” FACC, ECF No.

                                  21   195. GFI responded with a notice explaining that, because WFG filed this amendment without

                                  22   leave of court and while the instant motion to dismiss was still pending, the Court should not

                                  23   consider the FACC. ECF No. 207. GFI’s objection concerning WFG’s filing the FACC without

                                  24   leave is not well taken for reasons explained above, but the fact that the FACC was filed before

                                  25   the Court ruled on the instant motion does present a complication. However, the changes in the

                                  26   FACC do not alter the result of the analysis below, so the Court will treat the FACC as the

                                  27   operative pleading for purposes of this Order.

                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION

                                            Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD        Document 247         Filed 09/09/25      Page 6 of 9



                                                B.     Equitable Estoppel
                                   1
                                                GFI contends that equitable estoppel applies to WFG’s counterclaims because they rely on
                                   2
                                       the Olsons’ relationship with WFG—i.e., the Agent Agreement at the heart of the arbitration
                                   3
                                       between WFG and the Olsons—and on Agent Agreements WFG entered into with other ex-agents
                                   4
                                       that have since left to join GFI. The FACC asserts seven causes of action: tortious interference
                                   5
                                       with contract, trade libel, libel per se, fraud, unjust enrichment, civil conspiracy, and unfair
                                   6
                                       competition in violation of Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq. FACC ¶¶ 258–318. According
                                   7
                                       to GFI, each of these causes of action depends on terms of the Agent Agreement to state a claim,
                                   8
                                       so WFG may not avoid the Arbitration Agreement that forms part of the same agreement.3
                                   9
                                                On the face of the FACC, that appears to be true. The FACC is replete with references to
                                  10
                                       the Agent Agreement and agents’ breaches of that contract. See, e.g., id. ¶¶ 3 (“GFI convinced
                                  11
                                       numerous WFGIA independent contractor agents to breach their Agreements with WFGIA by
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       diverting independent contractor agents, new recruits, and commission streams away from
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       WFGIA and to GFI . . . .”), 7 (“GFI’s entire growth model was based on unfair competition and
                                  14
                                       violations of dozens, if not hundreds, of WFGIA Agreements . . . .”), 34 (listing the non-
                                  15
                                       solicitation, confidentiality, and non-disparagement provisions of the Agent Agreement that
                                  16
                                       collectively form the Restrictive Covenants). The FACC’s causes of action center around an
                                  17
                                       alleged scheme in which the Olsons solicited WFG agents, took or induced others to take WFG’s
                                  18
                                       confidential information, and used such confidential information to compete with WFG through
                                  19
                                       GFI, all violations of the Agent Agreement. See id. ¶¶ 135–49 (alleging that WFG agents “were
                                  20
                                       still under contract with WFGIA . . . when they participated in [soliciting WFG’s agents to join
                                  21
                                       GFI] in violation of their Agreements with WFGIA”), 162–75 (alleging that “GFI has utilized its
                                  22

                                  23
                                       3
                                  24     WFG claims that, because the Arbitration Agreement is a separate document from the Agent
                                       Agreement, GFI’s equitable estoppel argument fails. Opp. at 22 n.4. Not so. WFG requires its
                                  25   agents to sign the Agent Agreement with the Arbitration Agreement in one integrated packet of
                                       documents. See ECF No. 26-4. As such, they are part of a unified transaction, and the Court will
                                  26   treat them as a single contract. See Cal. Civ. Code § 1642 (“Several contracts relating to the same
                                       matters, between the same parties, and made as parts of substantially one transaction, are to be
                                  27   taken together.”); see also Patterson-Ballagh Corp. v. Byron Jackson Co., 145 F.2d 786, 788 (9th
                                       Cir. 1944).
                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION
                                                                                        6
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 247         Filed 09/09/25       Page 7 of 9




                                   1   Anchor Leg Strategy to instruct double agents to access WFGIA’s protected networks and provide

                                   2   WFGIA’s confidential information to GFI” despite the fact that the Agent Agreement requires

                                   3   agents to “keep WFGIA confidential information confidential”), 176–86 (alleging that “WFGIA’s

                                   4   confidential information has permitted GFI to replicate WFGIA’s business, financial, and

                                   5   compensation models . . . [and] induce [agents] to violate their contract”).

                                   6          WFG does not dispute that the FACC references the Agent Agreement but argues that the

                                   7   viability of its claims does not necessarily rely on any provision in the contract. Opp. at 23–25.

                                   8   Indeed, for GFI’s reliance argument to succeed, “[WFG’s] claims themselves must intimately rely

                                   9   on the existence of the [Agent] Agreements, not merely reference them.” Kramer, 705 F.3d at

                                  10   1132. Here, it is not clear that WFG’s causes of action are dependent on the Agent Agreements.

                                  11   For example, although WFG refers to breaches of the Agent Agreement in stating its unfair

                                  12   competition claim, the claim could stand without those references. WFG alleges that other GFI
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   conduct, including “divert[ing] WFGIA customers,” and “tak[ing] WFGIA’s confidential

                                  14   information [in violation of the Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act]” also

                                  15   constitute unfair business practices. FACC ¶¶ 312–13. As another example, WFG’s trade libel

                                  16   and libel per se do not even reference the Agent Agreement at all, instead alleging that GFI made

                                  17   false and disparaging statements independent of the contracts. Id. ¶¶ 272–83.

                                  18          However, WFG cannot so easily plead around equitable estoppel. “In matters of equity,

                                  19   such as the application of equitable estoppel, it is the substance of the plaintiff's claim that counts,

                                  20   not the form of its pleading.” Franklin v. Cmty. Reg'l Med. Ctr., 998 F.3d 867, 875 (9th Cir.

                                  21   2021). WFG’s claims are inherently rooted in the contractual relationships it had with the Olsons

                                  22   and ex-agents that left to join GFI. That much is clear from the FACC’s introduction. WFG

                                  23   summarizes its counterclaims as “GFI convinced numerous WFGIA independent contractor agents

                                  24   to breach their Agreements with WFGIA” (FACC ¶ 3), and “GFI’s entire growth model was based

                                  25   on unfair competition and violations of dozens, if not hundreds, of WFGIA Agreements” (id. ¶ 7).

                                  26   These alleged breaches of Agent Agreements and the resulting damages WFG incurred form the

                                  27   basis of WFG’s counterclaims, even if the FACC does not explicitly say so.

                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION
                                                                                          7
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD          Document 247          Filed 09/09/25   Page 8 of 9




                                   1          Take, for example, WFG’s claim for unjust enrichment. WFG alleges, among other things,

                                   2   that “GFI . . . did not compensate or provide any consideration to WFGIA in exchange for . . .

                                   3   unlawful solicitation of WFGIA independent contractor agents through its theft of WFGIA’s

                                   4   confidential information and disparagement campaign.” Id. ¶ 301. WFG does not refer to the

                                   5   Agent Agreement to state a claim for unjust enrichment. But in doing so, it cannot avoid evoking

                                   6   the non-solicitation, confidentiality, and non-disparagement provisions of the Agent Agreement,

                                   7   the legality of which is a core issue in the arbitration between WFG and the Olsons. See ECF Nos.

                                   8   191-4, 198-4. In fact, the FACC does not explain how solicitation of WFG’s agents could be

                                   9   “unlawful” or how WFG’s confidential information is entitled to protection without the effect of

                                  10   the Restrictive Covenants in the Agent Agreement. Thus, even if WFG’s counterclaims do not

                                  11   expressly rely on the Agent Agreement, they are at least “intimately founded in and intertwined

                                  12   with” it. See Kramer, 705 F.3d at 1128 (equitable estoppel applies “when a signatory must rely on
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the terms of the written agreement in asserting its claims against the nonsignatory or the claims

                                  14   are ‘intimately founded in and intertwined with’ the underlying contract” (emphasis added)).

                                  15          Waymo LLC v. Uber Techs., Inc., which WFG cites in opposition, is inapposite. 252 F.

                                  16   Supp. 3d 934 (N.D. Cal. 2017). In Waymo, the court declined to apply equitable estoppel because

                                  17   the relevant claims neither relied upon nor were intimately founded in or intertwined with the

                                  18   underlying contract. See id. at 937. But that decision was based on the fact that Waymo

                                  19   “expressly forswore reliance on [the agreements] to prove up its claims.” Id. at 938. Not so here.

                                  20   WFG’s counterclaims do not invoke provisions of the Agent Agreement to state a claim, but they

                                  21   are inextricably tied with the Agent Agreement and the obligations it imposes on its signatories. It

                                  22   would be difficult to disentangle WFG’s counterclaims from issues that are already properly in

                                  23   arbitration, including whether provisions of the Agent Agreement are void and whether the Olsons

                                  24   (and other agents) breached that agreement. As such, WFG is equitably estopped from preventing

                                  25   its counterclaims against GFI from being arbitrated.

                                  26
                                  27

                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER COMPELLING ARBITRATION

                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD         Document 247       Filed 09/09/25   Page 9 of 9



                                       IV.    CONCLUSION
                                   1
                                              For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS GFI’s motion to compel WFG’s
                                   2
                                       counterclaims to arbitration.
                                   3
                                              IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  13

                                  14          Before the Court is Plaintiff Global Financial Impact, LLC’s (“GFI”) motion to stay

                                  15   discovery. ECF No. 232. GFI seeks to stay discovery related to Defendant World Financial

                                  16   Group Insurance Agency, LLC’s (“WFG”) counterclaims during the pendency of GFI’s motion to

                                  17   dismiss, stay, or compel arbitration, ECF No. 190.

                                  18          Courts have broad discretion in controlling discovery. Little v. City of Seattle, 863 F.2d

                                  19   681, 685 (9th Cir. 1988). Courts routinely exercise that discretion to grant stays pending

                                  20   resolution of a motion to compel arbitration, because if that motion is granted, the arbitrator will

                                  21   have the authority to determine the nature and scope of discovery. See Mahamedi IP L., LLP v.

                                  22   Paradice & Li, LLP, No. 5:16-CV-02805, 2017 WL 2727874, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 14, 2017)

                                  23   (collecting cases); Stiener v. Apple Computer, Inc., No. C 07-4486 SBA, 2007 WL 4219388, at *1

                                  24   (N.D. Cal. Nov. 29, 2007). A short stay often will serve the parties’ interests in conserving

                                  25   resources and the court’s interest in securing just, speedy, and inexpensive resolutions of cases

                                  26   before it. Stiener, 2007 WL 4219388, at *1; see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 1.

                                  27          The same holds true here. Engaging in fulsome discovery while GFI’s motion to compel

                                  28   Case No.: 5:24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER STAYING DISCOVERY
                                                                                         1
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD          Document 237         Filed 08/06/25     Page 2 of 2




                                   1   arbitration is pending could undermine the potential efficiencies of arbitration and lead to

                                   2   inconsistent results. Further, the Court is not persuaded that a stay would significantly prejudice

                                   3   WFG. WFG asserts several arguments in opposition to GFI’s motion to stay discovery, but none

                                   4   are availing. ECF No. 234. Notably, WFG cites concealment and spoliation of evidence by GFI.

                                   5   Though the Court does not condone such discovery misconduct if it is occurring, WFG has not

                                   6   proffered enough evidence at this time to show that the risk of concealment or spoliation of

                                   7   evidence outweighs the benefits of a temporary discovery stay.

                                   8          For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS GFI’s motion to stay discovery. All

                                   9   discovery related to WFG’s counterclaims shall be stayed until the Court issues a ruling on GFI’s

                                  10   motion to dismiss, stay, or compel arbitration, ECF No. 190.
